idiom_name: unexported token type in the owning package (package-scoped grant); internal/ subtree for a narrower importer set
implementation_notes: Go's only access forms are exported and unexported, and the Go 1.4 release notes are explicit that 'the Go language does not have the power to enforce this distinction' - but an unexported token type is still a real compile-time boundary: another package cannot name the type ('name key not exported by package a') and cannot call the restricted method without a value ('cannot use nil as a key value'). Values do travel, so a caller that receives a token from an exported function can pass it on, which is the delegation mechanism - but any exported constructor of the token (a MakeKey function, an exported field) hands the grant to the world, so keep the token unexported and keep the authorised collaborator in the same package. Where the grantee is a subtree rather than a package, place the implementation under an internal/ directory: the go command then refuses imports from outside the tree rooted at its parent, although that is a toolchain rule, not a language rule.
code_sketch:
package pool

type key struct{}                          // unexported: no other package can name or forge it

func (p *Pool) releaseInternal(k key) { }  // callable only by code in package pool

func (p *Pool) Shutdown() { p.releaseInternal(key{}) }   // authorised collaborator

// elsewhere: p.releaseInternal(...)  // compile error - no value of type key obtainable
pitfalls: An exported function returning the token type, or an exported token field, quietly makes the grant package-external: delegation degenerates into forging.
The unexported-parameter trick makes exported methods awkward for documentation and linters; keep such methods unexported and route real API through a package-internal path.
internal/ constrains importers only, is enforced by the go command at build time, and does not stop reflection or unsafe code already inside the subtree.
